interest: Shows early-1930s State Department review of Japanese emigration policy, its Manchuria failures, and shift toward Latin America.
keywords: Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of 1911
Law for the Protection of Emigrants
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.5611) comprises State Department correspondence and an extensive research memorandum produced between March 1932 and April 1933 concerning the policy and practice of the Japanese government regarding the emigration of laborers to the United States. Originating in the Treaty Division under Chief Charles M. Barnes as part of historical research into the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation, the primary memorandum—drafted by William V. Whittington—traces Japanese emigration policy from Foreign Minister Count Jutarō Komura's 1910 'policy of concentration' (directing emigrants to Manchuria and Korea) and the Gentlemen's Agreement through the passage of the U.S. Immigration Act of 1924 and up to 1931. The study analyzes Japanese statutory frameworks, notably the 1896 Law for the Protection of Emigrants and subsequent Foreign Office ordinances, examines diplomatic and consular reporting from Tokyo and Kobe regarding emigration statistics and population pressures, and highlights Japan's shifting demographic focus toward South America (particularly Brazil) following exclusion from the United States and the failure of Japanese agriculturalists to compete effectively with Chinese labor in Manchuria.

keywords: Law for the Protection of Emigrants
subfiles.summary: This extensive Treaty Division memorandum investigates the policy and administrative practice of the Japanese government concerning the emigration of Japanese laborers to the United States. It outlines Count Komura's 1910 'policy of concentration' aimed at directing surplus population to Korea and Manchuria while strictly controlling migration to the United States under the Gentlemen's Agreement and the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation. The document details the legislative and regulatory mechanisms employed by Tokyo, notably the 1896 Law for the Protection of Emigrants and subsequent Foreign Office ordinances, confirming that strict central passport controls remained actively enforced despite protests from provincial governors. Drawing upon reports and statistics from U.S. diplomatic and consular posts in Tokyo and Kobe, the memorandum traces the sharp drop in emigration to the U.S. after the Immigration Act of 1924, highlights the failure of Japanese colonization in Manchuria due to competition with Chinese laborers, and explains the resulting redirection of Japanese emigrants toward South America, particularly Brazil.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Whittington on Policy and Practice of Japanese Government in Relation to the Emigration of Japanese Laborers to the United States
